using Prezi over the other software solutions?
Let’s start by looking at how Prezi works.
The first thing you need to understand about Prezi, is it’s an online presentation application
that allows you to create presentations using a single canvas which contains frames.
Each frame contains the content you would normally add to a slide.
If you click on a frame, you zoom in to the content. Just like a slide, each frame can
contain the content of your pitch deck.
The frames are dispersed around the canvas and then linked via a path.
Whereas with slides you traditionally tend to present your story chronologically.
What I always stress in any pitch deck is to create a storyline and work progressively
from one point to the next to develop a story that sequentially covers the key points of
your business. Prezi certainly gives you that ability however you have to think of your
presentation a little differently.
If you have levels of information within that frame that need to be clicked on to be revealed,
you could be creating an issue when it becomes a standalone presentation that you send out
to investors.
If investors are randomly flipping through your pitch deck without you there, they may
miss some crucial points and your storyline will seem muddled.
Another thing you need to avoid is having too many points within points. Zooming in
and out again will make your potential investors dizzy.

Want to make your Prezi presentation easy to share? You can instantly
generate a QR code that links directly to your presentation — no typing, just scan and go.
Here’s how to add one. In the Prezi Present editor,
click the Share button in the top right corner. Select Insert QR code, and Prezi automatically
creates a code that links to your presentation. Click Insert to place it anywhere on your canvas,
or download it to add to posters, slides, or emails.
If you want the QR code to point somewhere else, replace the default link with any URL — like a
feedback form or event page. Now try scanning the QR code
yourself to check how it looks! That’s it — your audience can now
open your presentation in seconds. Try adding a QR code in Prezi today.

Want to turn your Prezi presentation into a video? Here's how.
Click the arrow next to the Present button in the top right corner and select "Record as a video."
Choose how you want to appear—either next to your content with the background removed,
or just add voice-over narration. If you're appearing on camera,
allow camera access when prompted. Your background will automatically disappear,
putting you right alongside your content.
Adjust your frames so nothing covers your face while presenting. Use “Detach content
from frame” to resize objects and move elements around to create space for yourself on screen.
Don't forget to add presenter notes to help you stay on track while recording.
Ready? Hit Record and present through your frames. Use the keyboard shortcuts to switch
between different views as you go. When you're done, trim your video,
add a title, and save it. Share it as a link or download it as an MP4.
Want a pro tip? Download the Prezi Video desktop app from your dashboard and record your video in
HD without time limits, or go live with your presentation on Zoom, Teams, or Google Meet.
That's it! Now go create something amazing with Prezi Present and Prezi Video.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to create a simple prei style zoom
effect in PowerPoint. This is a
fantastic technique that allows you to
add dynamic motion to your
presentations, making them more engaging
and visually appealing. So, let's dive
into the process and see how we can
achieve this effect seamlessly. First,
you'll want to open PowerPoint and start
a new presentation. If you already have
PowerPoint open, great. You can either
create a brand new presentation or use
an existing one that you'd like to add
these effects to. Once that's ready,
we'll be inserting a large background
image or slide. Think of this as your
canvas for the project. It's important
to have a wide, captivating image that
can easily accommodate text or other
graphics without feeling cluttered.
Next, add your content, shapes, text, or
additional images right on top of the
background. These elements are vital as
they will be the focus of your zoom
effect.
Carefully arrange them to ensure they
are both visually appealing and easy to
read from a distance. This setup is
crucial because each element will be
highlighted, and you want to ensure your
audience clearly sees the message you're
conveying. Once your elements are in
place, it's time to duplicate the slide
for each step of your zoom effect. You
might be wondering why we do this. It's
because each duplicate will act as a
separate stage in the zoom journey. For
example, if you want to zoom in on three
different areas, you'll need three
duplicates. Each duplicate will help
simulate movement as we apply effects.
Now, on each duplicated slide, enlarge
the area you wish to zoom into. This can
be done by scaling or cropping. This
step is essential as it allows you to
isolate specific parts of your canvas
that you want to draw attention to. For
instance, you might want to zoom in on a
section of text or a particular image.
And scaling or cropping brings these
details into focus. To enhance the
movement between your slides, we will
apply smooth transitions such as the
morph transition. The morph transition
is particularly effective for this
purpose because it creates the illusion
of zooming and panning. It's essential
to ensure the effect is smooth and
engaging and morph helps achieve this
seamlessly by automatically animating
the shift between slides.
Finally, take some time to preview the
presentation. This preview is critical
as it allows you to see the prei style
zoom effect in action and ensure
everything runs smoothly. Check for any
inconsistencies or awkward transitions
and make tweaks as necessary. And that's
how you create a simple prey zoom effect
in PowerPoint.

transform your presentations into
visually compelling stories that
captivate your audience's attention.

Hey, Yiannis here and you're in the
right place if you want to learn about
creating line charts in Prezi Design.
They're perfect for displaying change
over time and visualizing time series
data. And with Prezi Design, you can
create regular line charts as well as
line charts with margins of error.
Here's how.
In the Prezi Design editor, select add
chart in the left side toolbar.
You'll find the line charts in the
sidebar.
To add a line chart to your project,
hover over its thumbnail and select
insert or drag and drop it onto the
canvas.
You'll see the chart appear with some
placeholder data. Double-click on the
chart to open the data sheet. The
placeholders are meant for you to see
the proper data formatting.
Enter the time series in column A and
then dedicate each following column to
the categories you'll be comparing. Type
in the values representing each category
in the cells opposite of the time
series. If you're creating an error
margin chart, use column A for the time
series. Enter the name of the group
you're comparing in column E, then
provide the values in column B and the
negative and positive error margins in
columns C and D respectively. To compare
the error margin to another group, enter
all the same time series in column A
below the existing ones and fill out the
other cells in the same way as with the
first group.
To add your data, you can type it in
manually or copy and paste it from an
external spreadsheet. You can also
select upload file and upload an Excel
or CSV file.
Select add Google Drive document to
connect your chart to a Google
spreadsheet and ensure live data
updates.
It's also possible to use a JSON feed
URL by selecting add JSON feed, as well
as source your data from one of the five
online databases available from this
drop-down.
Once you've added the data to your
chart, it's time to customize it.
Quick tip, to resize the chart, simply
hover over one of its sides or corners
and click and drag your mouse in any
direction.
After selecting the chart on the canvas,
its editing options will appear in the
settings panel on the right. Click on
the tabs to access them.
Under chart properties, you can choose
to display the values on the chart,
smooth on the curves of the lines,
let others download your data, and more.
From the color tab, you can change the
chart's colors, as well as adjust the
weight and style of the lines.
The axis and grid tab makes it possible
to adjust the look of the grid, give
titles to the axes, adjust the labels,
set intervals, and more.
Under fonts, you'll be able to adjust
the size and color of the font and
change the font itself.
Select advanced settings to adjust
specific text elements.
Click on legend to turn it on or off and
adjust its positioning.
Use the tool tips tab to enable or
disable them. If you're sharing the
chart online, we advise to keep them on
for better data readability.
Data format lets you add a prefix and a
suffix to your values and make other
adjustments to your data.
Last but not least, use the
accessibility tab to add a label and a
description to your chart to make it
more accessible for the viewers who are
using screen readers.
If you haven't already, add a title to
your chart with one of the text elements
available under add text. Don't forget
to mention the source of your data.
Now that the chart's ready, it's time to
download it. Access the download page in
the top right corner.
Here you'll see five download formats.
PNG, JPEG, and PDF for static downloads,
as well as a GIF and MP4 option. The
last two will come in handy if your line
chart has several tabs and you'd like
them to play out one by one.
The sharing options can also be accessed
from the top right corner by selecting
share.
You can keep your project private or
make it accessible for everyone on the
web. Share the link with others for them
to view your chart.
On the view page, you can access the
embed code by selecting embed under the
content. Copy the code and use it on
your website for the chart to appear
with all of its interactive features
intact. That's it. Go to prezi.com to
start creating your own interactive line
charts and much more.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to reorder slides in Prezi. If your
presentation story doesn't quite flow or
you just want to tighten up the
sequence, reordering your frames, what
Prezi often treats like slides, is quick
and intuitive.
I'll walk you through the process and
share a few helpful tips so you feel
confident making changes without losing
your rhythm.
First, open your Prezi in the editor.
You'll know you're in the right place
when you can see your canvas and all the
content you've created.
On the left side of the editor, there's
a timeline panel that shows the path
your presentation will follow. If you
don't see that panel, it's likely
hidden.
Look for a small tab along the left edge
of the screen and click it to open the
timeline.
This panel is your control center for
ordering your content.
Inside that timeline, you'll see your
frames or steps displayed as a vertical
list of thumbnails.
Each thumbnail is a snapshot of a frame
on your canvas and they appear in the
exact order your presentation will play.
Think of this like a storyboard. Top to
bottom equals first to last. To reorder,
click and hold on any frame thumbnail
you want to move.
As you drag it up or down the list,
you'll notice the other thumbnails shift
to make space.
Pay attention to the small numbers next
to each thumbnail. Those numbers
represent the presentation order and
update as you adjust positions.
When you've dragged the frame to the
spot where you want it to appear, simply
release your mouse.
That's it. Your new order is set.
A couple of quick tips while you're
moving things around. If you
accidentally drop a frame in the wrong
place, just click it again and drag it
to the correct spot.
It won't affect the content inside the
frame, only the order in which it
appears.
Also, consider the narrative.
Prezi shines when you lead viewers from
big picture context down into details
and your timeline order should support
that journey.
You can rearrange as much as you like
until the flow feels right.
Remember, changing the order in this
timeline changes the path your
presentation follows when you present.
That means your zooms, transitions, and
the sequence of ideas will all follow
the new arrangement.
Once you've set the order, you're ready
to deliver a presentation that feels
more logical, engaging, and easy to
follow.
And that's how to reorder slides in
Prezi.
Open the editor, show the left timeline
if it's hidden, locate your frames, drag
and drop them into the correct order,
and release to confirm.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to add hyperlinks in PREI.
Adding hyperlinks is a great way to
enrich your presentations and connect
your audience with additional resources
or related content, making your work
more interactive and engaging. To get
started, open your presentation within
the Prei editor. If you haven't done so
already, log into your Prei account and
choose the presentation you'd like to
enhance with hyperlinks.
Once you have your presentation open,
the next thing you'll want to do is
decide which piece of text or object you
want to turn into a hyperlink. This
could be a specific word, a phrase, or
even a visual element like an image or
icon that you believe will complement
your presentation with an external link.
Once you've identified the text or
object, you'll need to select it. If
it's text, simply click and drag your
mouse over the portion you wish to link.
If it's an object, just click on it once
to select it. You'll notice that once
the item is selected, editing options
will appear around it. This is your cue
that you're ready to move on to the next
step. Now, let's incorporate the
hyperlink. Look for the hyperlink icon
in the toolbar. The toolbar should
either be at the top of your screen or
may appear near the selected text or
object depending on your interface. The
icon typically looks like a chain link
representing the connection you're about
to make between your presentation and
the internet. Once you've clicked on the
hyperlink icon, a field will appear
prompting you to paste the URL you want
to link to. Make sure you have the
correct URL copied beforehand and paste
it into the designated field. It's
essential that this URL is accurate
because this is the link your audience
will follow when interacting with your
presentation.
After pasting the URL, confirm and apply
the hyperlink to the selected text or
object. Usually, this entails clicking a
button labeled apply or something
similar which will finalize the action.
At this point, your hyperlink is
successfully integrated into your prey
presentation. Before you wrap up, it's
important to test the link in present
mode. Click the present or preview
button to simulate what your audience
will experience. Navigate to the
hyperlink and click on it to ensure it
redirects to the correct web address.
This step is crucial to catch any
potential errors and guarantee a
seamless presentation experience. And
that's how you add hyperlinks in prei.
By following these steps, you can enrich
your presentations with valuable content
from the web, creating a more dynamic
and informative experience for your
audience.

presenting.

Every great tale has the power to captivate, inspire, and
transport us to new worlds.
But what truly sets apart the remarkable storytellers, the ones who
can effortlessly weave narratives that resonate deeply with their audience?
In this video, we'll explore the art of storytelling, uncovering
the five essential steps that pave the way to mastery.
So without further ado, let's dive right in and unlock the power of storytelling.
Skillful storytellers craft their stories with a specific outcome in mind.
They may aim to inspire, drive change, or raise awareness about an issue.
That's why the first step towards storytelling mastery is defining
the purpose of your story.
Ask yourself these questions.
What message do you wish to convey?
What takeaway do you want your audience to have?
And lastly, why do you feel it's important to share this message?
By answering these questions, you'll have a clearer understanding of how your
story should unfold, and what visuals or structure you should apply to amplify it.
When it comes to story time, the ultimate goal is to establish a profound bond with
your audience through connection points.
This bond can be built on similar viewpoints, challenges,
emotions, and other experiences.
It is through this connection that your message can be effectively
delivered, igniting conversations that can lead to amazing discoveries
and meaningful relationships.
To lay the ground for these connection points, first you
need to understand your audience.
You need to familiarize yourself with the demographics and interest to identify
connection points that resonate with them.
Next, tap into universal emotions by highlighting the feelings experienced
by the characters in your story.
This allows the audience to connect on a deeper level and
improve their own engagement.
Lastly, you want to identify and incorporate themes or values that
resonate with a wide range of people, such as love, friendship, personal
growth, or overcoming adversity.
This will help your audience to find connection points based on
shared experiences and values.
By considering these three factors, you'll be able to lay the foundation
for deep trust, engagement, and interest in your story.
To amplify engagement and understanding, find visual materials
that allow your audience to dive deeper into your story world.
That's where Prezi can help you create dynamic presentations
that will engage your audience.
With its zooming capabilities, multimedia elements, and visual story mapping.
Prezi enables you to guide your audience through a captivating
and memorable narrative.
By incorporating interactive elements and pathways, you can make your
audience feel involved in the story.
To demonstrate how a Prezi presentation can enhance storytelling, let's
look at two different presentations.
The first Prezi presents a captivating exploration of one of the most
significant chapters in American history.
With its impressive visuals and animation, the presentation conveys
the struggles, victory, and lasting impacts of the civil rights movement.
From the very beginning, it draws the viewer's attention
with dynamic opening animation.
The first slide sets the tone with a powerful image, immersing the
audience in the historical context.
Animations like subtle transitions, zooming, and movement of elements
bring the content to life, making it more engaging and memorable.
The second presentation provides a comprehensive guide to developing a clear
and impactful organizational framework.
It uses relatable narratives and real world examples to explain the importance
and benefits of defining purpose, vision, mission, values, and key measures.
This technique helps the viewers connect emotionally with the content and
understand its practical applications.
And the interactive elements encourage active participation and engagement.
The art of storytelling can only be truly mastered through
constant practice and learning.
By regularly practicing your speech and using the following methods,
you can ensure that you look and feel confident in your delivery.
First, start with reading your speech aloud to familiarize
yourself with the content.
As you become more comfortable, you want to aim to gradually transition
from reading it to memorizing some key points and transitions.
Then, practice your speech until you can deliver it fluently.
Second, if you plan to incorporate visual aids, integrate them
into your practice sessions.
Practice coordinating your speech with visuals and maintaining
a smooth flow of information.
Third, value constructive feedback.
Try practicing in front of your friends, family, or colleagues, and
ask them to evaluate you on clarity, coherence, and overall impact.
Lastly, be open to improvisation.
Allow room for spontaneity and adaptability during
your actual presentation.
This flexibility will help you connect better with your audience
and respond to their reactions.
Remember, effective speech practice is not just about memorizing words, but
also about capturing the essence of your story and engaging your audience.
The last key step in becoming a great storyteller is to simply
trust your audience, and here's why.
First of all, trusting your audience opens the door for
meaningful dialogue and feedback.
By encouraging questions, comments, and discussions, you can create
an environment where your audience feels comfortable expressing their
thoughts and sharing their own stories.
This exchange of ideas fosters a sense of community.
And second of all, when you trust your audience, you're inviting them to actively
participate in the storytelling process.
This connection fosters a sense of authenticity and openness, enabling
a deeper emotional resonance between you and your listeners.
So being open and responsive and creating a safe space for your
listeners will cultivate a healthy and engaging environment that will
lead to meaningful conversations.
And there you have it.
The five key elements to master the art of storytelling by defining your
purpose, finding connection points, making a visual impact with Prezi,
practicing your delivery and building safe space for your listeners, you'll
be on your way to deliver highly impactful speech or presentation.
If you enjoyed learning, make sure to like and share this video with
your friends, family, or colleagues.
I'm Naba from Prezi's Marketing Team and I wish you success
delivering impactful stories.
Have fun and see you next time.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to add links in prei. By the end,
you'll be able to turn text and visuals
into clickable pathways that guide your
audience to websites, resources, and
more without breaking the flow of your
presentation. To begin, open your
presentation in the presi editor. You
want to be in edit mode so you can
interact with the content on your
canvas.
Once you're there, click to select the
item you want to link. This can be a
line of text or an object such as an
image, icon, shape, GIF, or chart.
When something is selected, Prei shows a
contextual toolbar so you can modify it.
If you're linking text, place your
cursor in the text box and type or paste
the full URL. For example,
https-acample.com.
Preezy recognizes full web addresses and
converts them into clickable links right
inside the text. Pasting is often the
best approach to avoid typos and missing
characters. Make sure the URL includes
the https
uh sas prefix and that there are no
extra spaces before or after it. If you
only want a specific word or phrase
linked, highlight that portion before
pasting the URL so the link applies to
just that selection. Clear, descriptive
link text helps your audience understand
exactly where the link will take them.
If you're linking an object instead of
text, keep that object selected and look
for the insert link icon in the toolbar
that appears. It typically looks like a
small chain link. Click it to open a
field where you can enter your link.
This is your spot to paste or type the
full URL. Again, use the complete
address with https
and double check that the domain is
spelled correctly.
After you enter it, the object becomes a
clickable hotspot in your presentation.
So when viewers click it, they go
directly to your chosen destination. If
you later replace the image or adjust
your layout, just reselect the object
and update the URL in the same place.
A few quick tips to keep everything
smooth. Copy links directly from your
browser's address bar to prevent stray
characters. Use stable public URLs that
your audience can access without special
permissions. And keep your linked items
visually clear so people know they're
interactive. Consistency matters, too.
Use the same linking style across your
presentation to make navigation feel
natural. And that's it. Open your prei
in the editor. Select your text or
object and add the full URL either by
typing it into the text box for text or
by using the insert link icon for
objects. With these simple steps, your
prei becomes more engaging, informative,
and interactive.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to lock objects in Prey.
Locking objects is a simple way to
protect your layout so elements don't
shift around while you're editing or
presenting. It's especially useful for
backgrounds, logos, or carefully aligned
graphics that you want to keep exactly
in place, even when you're working
quickly or collaborating with others.
First, open your prey presentation in
the editor. Make sure you're in edit
mode and not presenting so you can
interact with the canvas and your
elements. Give the page a second to load
fully and zoom to the area where you'll
be working so you can clearly see the
items you want to secure. Next, select
the object you want to lock. Click once
to highlight it. You'll see a selection
outline that confirms it's active. If
you need to lock more than one item,
select multiple objects before locking.
You can do this by holding down the
modifier key your device uses for multi
select or by dragging a selection box
around the items.
Take a moment to confirm you've got
exactly what you need highlighted. This
is a great time to double check
alignment and spacing because once the
objects are locked, they won't move
until you unlock them. Now, right click
on the selected object or group of
objects to open the context menu. If
you're on a trackpad, use a secondary
click gesture. In the menu that appears,
click lock. The change takes effect
immediately. There's no extra
confirmation step, so it's quick and
straightforward. With the object locked,
it's now fixed in place. You won't be
able to drag it, resize it, or delete it
accidentally. This is perfect for
keeping your base layout untouched while
you focus on editing text, adding
images, or adjusting your presentation
path. If you try to move a locked item,
nothing will happen, which is exactly
what you want when you're working under
a deadline or switching between many
elements on the canvas.
A few tips as you work. Lock
foundational elements first, like
background images, frames, and brand
assets. That way, you build on a stable
base as you design. When collaborating,
mention to your teammates which items
are locked to avoid confusion. And
remember to save your work periodically
so the locked state is preserved along
with your other edits. That's it. Open
your presentation in the editor, select
the objects you want to protect,
rightclick, and choose lock. It's a
small step that delivers big piece of
mind while you

[music] set a custom size and location.

your own.

delete your frames at any time.
Duplicate frames by selecting and
clicking control or command D.
If you want to move the content inside a
frame or delete the frame only, right
click and select detach content from
frame.
Tip: You can adjust the zooming effect
by creating larger frames. If your
frames are very small, it can disorient
your audience. Consider also placing the
frames near each other so you're not
jumping from one side of the canvas to

Welcome to our channel. Today, we how to
use Prezi for effective presentations
abroad easy tutorial step-by-step
clearly.
Open your web browser and navigate to
the Prezi website.
If you don't already have an account,
click on the sign up button and create
one.
Once logged in, select create new Prezi
to start a new presentation.
Choose a template that suits your topic
and audience.
Prezi offers a variety of visually
engaging templates.
After selecting a template, familiarize
yourself with the editing interface.
On the left panel, you'll find options
to add text, images, and videos.
Click on the text box to add your main
content.
Use concise language to ensure clarity
and engagement.
To add images, click on insert and
choose image.
You can upload images from your device
or find them through the Prezi library.
When adding videos, remember to keep
them relevant to your presentation.
Utilize the path feature to organize the
flow of your presentation.
This feature allows you to navigate
through your slides seamlessly.
Consider adding zoom animations to
highlight key points.
This will create a more dynamic viewing
experience for your audience.
Regularly preview your presentation to
check for coherence and visual appeal.
Once you're satisfied, click on the
present button to view your presentation
in full screen.
Make sure to practice your delivery with
the Prezi format.
This will help you become familiar with
navigating between sections.
Finally, when you're ready, share your
Prezi presentation with your audience.
You can choose to present live or share
a link for remote viewing.
If the page does not load, refresh the
browser or try again in a private or
incognito window.
Make sure you are using the correct
email address, then retype it carefully
to to small typos.
If your password is not accepted, use
the reset option and create a new strong
password you can remember.
Check your spam folder for verification
or security emails, then complete any
requested confirmation steps.
Enable two-factor authentication if
available to improve account security
and reduce unauthorized access risk.
After signing in, review your profile
details so your contact information and
settings are accurate and current.
If you see an error message, note it
down and try again after restarting your
device and internet connection.

step-by-step tech guides.

In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to create a customer journey map in
prei. This process will help you
visualize the path your customers take
from their first interaction with your
brand all the way to their post-purchase
experience.
With clear sections and engaging
visuals, a customer journey map can be
an invaluable tool for understanding and
optimizing your customers experience.
Let's get started by opening Prei and
creating a new presentation. Prei is a
powerful platform that offers a dynamic
way of capturing and presenting ideas
and it's perfect for mapping out a
customer journey. Once you've opened
Prei, the first thing you need to do is
select a template. Look for one that has
clear sections or a flow style layout.
This will help you organize different
stages of the journey seamlessly and
ensure that the map is easy to follow.
Now once you have your template, add a
main topic and label it customer journey
map. This serves as the central point
from which all stages of the journey
flow. It acts as the anchor for the rest
of your map and helps anyone viewing it
understand its primary focus. Next, you
want to create subtopics for each stage
of the journey. These typically include
stages like awareness, consideration,
purchase, and retention. By dividing the
journey into these segments, you can
delve deeper into each part of the
customer experience and analyze it
thoroughly. The next step is to enrich
these subtopics with details. Add text,
icons, and visuals to describe the
customer actions and touch points within
each stage.
This could be anything from a customer
seeing an advertisement during the
awareness stage to contacting customer
service in the retention stage. Using
icons and visuals can make the map more
engaging and easier to interpret at a
glance. To give an additional layer of
depth, consider inserting emotion
indicators or identifying pain points.
These elements will illustrate the
customer's emotional journey as they
move through each stage, highlighting
areas where they might experience
frustration or delight. It's these
insights that can lead to tangible
improvements in your customer experience
strategy.
Finally, take advantage of Pre's unique
zoom paths. These allow you to guide
viewers smoothly from one stage of the
journey to the next, creating a
narrative flow that mimics the actual
progression through a customer journey.
Zoom paths can often make the
presentation more dynamic and keep the
audience engaged by focusing their
attention on one stage at a time. And
that's how you create a customer journey
map in Prei.
By visually mapping out every step, you
can gain valuable insights into your
customers experiences and pinpoint
opportunities for enhancing their
journey with your brand. Thank you for
watching and happy mapping.

In this video, we will show you how to
import PowerPoint presentations to
Prezi.
First of all, open your browser and go
to prezi.com. For the purpose of this
tutorial, we have already created an
account on Prezi.
Once you're logged in with your account,
click on the new Prezi button available
on the left-hand side. A new page will
open up in a new tab where you will be
asked to choose your template. For the
purpose of this tutorial, we will start
off with a blank Prezi.
You will notice a circle where you can
add a title. Since we want to add a
PowerPoint presentation, we will simply
delete this and make the Prezi blank.
Once you're done, go to the top and
click on the insert button. From the
drop-down menu, select the PowerPoint
option. As a result, a window will
appear from where you can open the
presentation that you want to import.
Once you've opened the PPT, you can
monitor the progress of the upload in
the right pane. Once the PowerPoint
slides have been downloaded, click on
the insert all button to add all of the
slides.
As soon as you click on the insert all
button, you'll be asked to choose a
layout for the slides. For the purpose
of this tutorial, we will choose the
caterpillar layout. You can add a path
between your slides by checking the
respective option. Click on the insert
button to insert the slides in a
particular layout into Prezi.
Click on the green tick mark if you're
satisfied with the insertion. You can
always zoom in and out of the different
circles, increase or decrease the text
box size, tilt the text boxes as per
your requirement, etc. Once you're done
with the changes, click on the present
button on the top left corner of the
page. As a result, a Prezi slideshow
will start in full screen. Click on the
arrow keys at the bottom to skip from
one graphic circle to another in the
same way you go from one slide to
another.

Transcription:
Slide decks are everywhere, in meetings,
classrooms, and training rooms across
every organization. But here's the
thing, being familiar doesn't mean being
used well. Their real value depends
entirely on how we design them and how
we use them.
A digital slide deck is simply a
sequence of visual slides created in
software. Think of tools like
PowerPoint, Google Slides, Keynote, or
Prezi.
In learning and development, slide decks
have proven remarkably enduring and they
remain widely used today.
They can support a live session with a
facilitator or stand alone as a
self-paced resource.
When learners work through a deck
without a live facilitator, we call that
asynchronous learning, contrasting with
live sessions where everyone learns
together in real-time.
Let's start with live learning because
that's where most of us meet slide decks
first. Slides support facilitation in
face-to-face, virtual, and hybrid
sessions. Hybrid simply means some
learners are in the room while others
join remotely online. In all three
settings, slides provide visual cues,
images, charts, and bullet points. These
cues reinforce what the facilitator is
saying, so learners hear it and see it.
Slides also give a session its structure
from start to finish. They keep the
facilitator and learners aligned to the
agenda and help everyone manage time.
When ideas get complex, slides can
display key points, models, and
diagrams. That visual support makes
explanation and discussion of difficult
concepts much easier.
The source is clear on one point here.
Uncluttered, visually engaging slides
are linked to better attention and
better retention.
But slide decks don't stop working when
the session ends. They also serve as
stand-alone resources for clear
communication and knowledge transfer.
Picture a people professional sharing a
strategic learning update with senior
stakeholders. A well-built deck
communicates the key messages without
anyone presenting it live.
Or, imagine a summary deck shared after
a workshop for asynchronous review.
Learners revisit the material in their
own time at their own pace.
Slide decks also work as bite-sized
resources. Think product overviews or
short procedural guides.
A new starter can open a five-slide
guide and follow a process step-by-step.
And decks can include interactive
elements, too. Embedded videos, polls,
and links to external resources, which
work especially well in platforms like
Zoom or Microsoft Teams.
So, how do we design slide decks that
actually help people learn? The first
principle is simplicity. Keep each slide
simple and focused. Limit the
information on every slide, so each
point is easy to digest. One clear idea
per slide beats five competing ideas
every time. The second principle is
consistency across the whole deck. A
consistent visual theme and clear
formatting help learners know where to
look. When every slide follows the same
visual logic, nothing distracts from the
content. The third principle is to use
visuals with real purpose. Diagrams,
flowcharts, and infographics are useful
when they genuinely aid understanding. A
flowchart can show a process more
clearly than a paragraph ever could.
But, the source includes an explicit
caution here, and it matters. Cluttered
slides can overwhelm learners and
distract from the key messages you want
to land. If a visual doesn't earn its
place on the slide, take it off. Now,
let's talk about accessibility, making
slides easier for all learners to engage
with. The source gives three practical
examples. Use high-contrast colors, so
text stands out clearly from the
background. Choose readable fonts at a
size everyone can actually see. And add
alt text to every visual in the deck.
Simply a description of the image for
anyone who can't see it.
For asynchronous use, think about what
context self-paced learners will need.
Narration, speaker notes, or written
explanations can add that missing
context and help learners revisit
complex topics whenever needed. So,
let's bring this together with four key
points. First, slide decks are flexible
tools used across learning and
development in many ways. Second, they
support both live facilitated sessions
and stand-alone self-paced learning.
Third, effective decks are simple,
focused, and visually helpful, never
cluttered or overloaded. And fourth,
accessible features plus added
explanation make decks far more useful
for self-paced learners.
The central message is this, slide decks
work best when they're clear,
purposeful, and accessible. Design them
to match how your learners will actually
use them, and they'll keep earning their
place.

Astronomers may have found one of the
largest hidden worlds beyond Pluto, and
it could eventually join the solar
system's small family of officially
recognized dwarf planets.
Welcome to the Automated Daily Space
News edition, the podcast created by
generative AI.
I'm Trent Teller. Today is October 28th,
2026.
We'll begin in our own cosmic
neighborhood before moving outward to an
interstellar visitor, an atmosphere that
should not have survived, the remains of
a dead planetary system, and a few
unusual possibilities at the edge of
modern physics.
This episode is brought to you by Stock
MVP. Stock MVP helps you invest like the
pros using data-driven insights. Find
the link in the episode notes.
Our first story comes from the distant
outskirts of the solar system.
Astronomers working with the Vera C.
Rubin Observatory have identified a
large icy object beyond Pluto.
For now, it carries the provisional
designation 2026 ED138,
and scientists are calling it a dwarf
planet candidate rather than a confirmed
dwarf planet.
Early estimates leave plenty of
uncertainty about its exact size, but
its brightness suggests it could rank
among the largest objects found in this
remote region.
The discovery is notable not only for
the object itself, but also for what it
says about Rubin Observatory. Its main
sky survey is designed to repeatedly
scan enormous areas of the heavens,
making it particularly good at catching
faint objects that slowly change
position.
ED138 may therefore be an early sign
that the outer solar system still has
major discoveries waiting for us.
Staying with nearby small worlds, the
European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft
has now distinguished the two asteroids
Didymos and Dimorphos as separate bodies
for the first time.
Until this latest image, the pair
appeared to Hera as one unresolved point
of light.
Dimorphos is especially important
because it was struck by NASA's DART
spacecraft in 2022, deliberately
changing its orbit around Didymos.
That experiment showed that a spacecraft
impact could alter an asteroid's motion.
Hera's job is to examine the aftermath
in detail and turn that successful
demonstration into a better understood
planetary defense technique.
Seeing both bodies separately confirms
that the spacecraft is closing in and
that its camera can begin following the
system directly.
The image is modest, but it marks a
meaningful transition from navigating
toward a distant target to studying the
actual site of humanity's first asteroid
deflection test.
Next, the James Webb Space Telescope has
examined material flowing from 3M/Atlas,
only the third confirmed interstellar
object ever observed passing through our
solar system.
Webb detected very small grains
containing water ice mixed with dark
rocky dust. That ice looks different
from the relatively clean ice found in
many familiar comets.
Surprisingly, however, its signature
resembles material seen on some icy
bodies beyond Neptune.
This creates an intriguing connection
between an object born around another
star and ancient material preserved in
our own outer solar system.
One comet cannot reveal how every
planetary system forms, but the
resemblance suggests that distant
systems may build icy worlds from a
familiar range of ingredients.
Interstellar objects offer rare physical
samples of other star systems, even
though we can only examine them remotely
as they race past.
In this case, the visitor appears
foreign and familiar at the same time.
Webb has also delivered a surprise from
a much hotter destination. TOI-561b
is a rocky exoplanet so close to its
star that its surface is thought to
contain molten rock. Astronomers would
normally expect radiation from the star
to strip such a world of its atmosphere
over time. Instead, observations
indicate that TOI-561b
may possess a substantial atmosphere
that reflects a remarkable amount of
incoming light and moves heat away from
the permanently illuminated side. One
possible explanation is a layer of
mineral clouds formed from vaporized
rock. In effect, those clouds could act
as a planetary sunscreen, leaving the
day side cooler than a bare surface
would be. This is not a potentially
habitable planet. Its environment is far
too extreme. Its importance lies in
challenging assumptions about how long
rocky planets can retain atmospheres. If
an atmosphere can survive here,
atmospheric evolution around other
close-orbiting worlds may be more varied
than current models suggest.
Another planetary system is showing
astronomers what can remain after a star
reaches the end of its life.
The white dwarf J1328-1450
is surrounded by two distinct rings of
gaseous debris with a gap between them.
Researchers think the structure is being
maintained by two surviving planetary
bodies moving on separate paths around
the stellar remnant.
One of those bodies may be comparable in
scale to a dwarf planet.
White dwarfs are the dense cores left
behind when stars like the sun shed
their outer layers.
That transition can destroy planets,
throw them into new orbits, or grind
smaller objects into debris.
The newly observed double ring system
suggests the aftermath can remain
surprisingly organized.
It also offers a distant preview of the
solar system's very long-term future.
The sun will not become a white dwarf
for billions of years,
but systems like this show that even
after a star's dramatic transformation,
some planetary bodies can survive and
continue shaping what remains.
Far beyond the local universe, Webb has
found the most distant known ring galaxy
named GS18660.
It is seen as it existed only about 2
billion years after the Big Bang.
A bright ring filled with young stars
surrounds the galaxy, and the leading
explanation is that a smaller companion
passed through it, compressing gas and
setting off a wave of star formation.
Astronomers have also detected a
possible companion and a bridge of gas
connecting the two, although more
observations will be needed to confirm
the full story.
Ring galaxies are uncommon in the nearby
universe, so finding one this early in
cosmic history suggests that dramatic
direct collisions were already producing
complex structures when the universe was
still young.
The discovery gives researchers another
way to test how quickly galaxies
assembled, interacted, and transformed
during that formative era.
Finally, a theoretical study has
considered a process that sounds like
the reverse of a familiar cosmic event.
We know that two black holes can merge.
The new calculations ask whether one
black hole could instead split into two.
Under normal conditions, the answer
remains no. The laws governing energy,
rotation, and black hole entropy
strongly oppose the process.
The researchers did, however, identify a
very narrow possible exception.
A black hole rotating close to the
maximum rate permitted by physics might
divide while giving the resulting pair
enough motion to separate rather than
immediately merge again.
>> [snorts]
>> This is a mathematical possibility, not
an observed event, and the researchers
have not shown that nature actually
produces such divisions. Still, the work
is useful because it tests the
boundaries of black hole physics. Even
an extreme loophole can reveal where
established theories remain firm and
where deeper ideas about gravity may
eventually be needed.

eine interaktive Startseite hast, wo du

fragst. Das ist so geil an Preziei. Ich
nenne das dialogorientiertes

simpelste, was wir hier machen können.
